newsitem.title: UK: Protestant head bids to ease N.Irish march tension.
newsitem.headline: Protestant head bids to ease N.Irish march tension.

text.p: The head of Northern Ireland's main Protestant marching brotherhood said on Friday his Orange Order colleagues should compromise over a controversial weekend parade that many in the province fear could end in violence.
"Grand Master" Robert Saulters said Orangemen should be given an assurance that they had a right to march on Sunday but should not opt to go through a sensitive Catholic zone.

"For the sake of peace that seems to be the only option left but I would hope that it would not be taken as weakness...We must have some kind of guarantee that it (the route) will not be closed to the brethren for all time," he told BBC radio.

Saulters stressed that the final decision on how the parade would be conducted lay with the Order's local branch in the town of Portadown, midway between Belfast and the border with Ireland, where sectarian tension is high.
Britain's minister for the province, Mo Mowlam, had talks on Thursday with security chiefs about the march and a Catholic counter-protest.
She wants to avoid a rerun of the chaos throughout Northern Ireland last year when the march was initially banned but allowed to proceed after four days of Protestant violence.
Mowlam is hoping for a last-minute deal between the pro-British Order and Irish nationalists objectors who plan to hold a "street festival" in the parade's path.
Without a compromise, Mowlam is expected to announce within 48 hours a ban on one or other of the events.
An outlawed pro-British Loyalist group has threatened to kill Catholics in the neighbouring Irish Republic if Britain bans the Orange parade.

Saulters is the first Orange leader publicly to back the compromise deal but there was no immediate sign that the Portadown leadership would embrace it. Saulters said that "at the end of the day it is the decision of the Portadown brethren."
He accused the leader of the Catholic objectors of intransigence and attacked the Irish government, which opposes the parade, for "interfering in Northern Ireland affairs".

Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern, who came to power last week, has made clear that he would be against any move by British troops and police to clear nationalist counter-demonstrators and force the march through.
Catholics regard members of the Order as Protestant supremacists and say that, as a minority in Portadown, they feel intimidated by the annual parade.
Orange leaders insist that Sunday's parade will be solemn and dignified, and held simply to celebrate their Protestant faith.

The controversy, coming in the runup to the climax to the climax of the Protestant "marching season", when sectarian feelings in both communities are traditionally brittle, is clouding Anglo-Irish attempts to end decades of guerrilla war.
Both nations feel that spillover violence from the march will further polarise majority Protestants and minority Catholics and hamper prospects for a political settlement.
The province has been tense for months because of a resurgent campaign by Irish Republican Army, which is fighting British rule, and sporadic retaliatory attacks by pro-British Loyalist extremists.
